question: In Europe, staff shortages at some air navigation service providers are causing serious delays, affecting the first flights of the day in particular. Initial delays disrupt the entire day: each minute lost can grow to as much as four minutes by the end of the day. In 2024, only 79% of these first-wave flights departed on time, with air traffic control delays shooting up by 31%.

Passengers directly bear the brunt – through missed connections, long waits and even cancellations. To ensure that first-wave flights depart and arrive on time, staffing numbers must be stepped up. 1.
Does the Commission intend to introduce a right to compensation or legal redress for airlines affected by the knock-on effects of poor performances by air navigation service providers?
Does the Commission intend to include those principles in a future European aviation strategy and/or though the revision of Regulation (EC) No 1008/2008 on the operation of air services?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.6.2025) 1. According to the rules governing the performance of air navigation service providers, Member States must set out incentives of financial nature for the achievement of binding national performance targets for air traffic control capacity in an effective and proportional manner, both for services to overflights and for services at and around airports.

Member States also have the obligation to implement penalties for infringements of the regulation by, amongst others, air navigation services providers. National supervisory authorities must enforce necessary corrective measures in the event of non-compliance. The Commission does not foresee further regulatory actions beyond those under the scope of Regulation (EU) 2024/28031 on the implementation of the Single Sky.

The Commission nonetheless underlines that the Court of Justice of the European Union in Case C-353/20 Skeyes2 has recognised a right for airspace users such as airlines to an effective remedy before the national courts against the air traffic services provider for any alleged failures by the latter in fulfilling its obligation to provide services. 2.

The Commission is relaunching the review of the Air Services Regulation3. One of the issues being looked at during that review is how to mitigate the impact of disruptions to air traffic control, in particular regarding overflights on air carriers’ freedom to provide services.
